title: Insurance interpretation: Coverage turned on application wording
desc: Separates judicial reflections on language from the holding, which rested on case-specific documents and binding law rather than LLM use.

kps.k: The supplied Snell material separates judicial reflections on interpretation from the grounds of decision; it does not establish a substantive proposal for using LLMs.
kps.d: Judge Newsom joins the court’s opinion in full and introduces a separate, experience-based proposal about interpreting legal instruments. The supplied excerpts stop before he explains that proposal. This material therefore establishes the interpretive context, not evidence of AI capabilities, a recommended judicial workflow or judicial reliance on AI. Any account of Snell’s role in the legal-AI debate must preserve that evidentiary limit.

qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: I write separately (and I’ll confess this is a little unusual1) simply to         pull back the curtain on the process by which I thought through         one of the issues in this case—and using my own experience here         as backdrop, to make a modest proposal regarding courts’         interpretations of the words and phrases used in legal instruments.
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The appellate court resolves coverage through the insurance application and binding state law, rather than deciding the ordinary meaning of landscaping.
kps.d: The district court concluded that landscaping did not encompass trampoline installation. The appellate court instead holds that Snell loses even under favorable readings of landscaping and causation: his application denied recreational-equipment work, and the trampoline’s classification as recreational equipment was undisputed. Snell argued that the application required express incorporation; the court followed the Alabama Supreme Court’s contrary statutory construction. Newsom personally questioned that construction but accepted its controlling force. The case illustrates why an interpretive question can motivate a concurrence without determining the outcome.

qs.q: Even taking the term “landscaping” as ambiguous,         construing it in Snell’s favor, and applying Alabama law’s broad         understanding of the causal term “arises out of,” Snell’s claim still         fails.
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: And we are bound by Alabama’s         interpretation of its own laws.
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The coverage ruling turns on a case-specific distinction between defining coverage and excluding otherwise covered work.
kps.d: The court treats the specified-operations provision as defining the policy’s boundaries, which places the burden of establishing coverage on Snell. It rejects his characterization of the provision as an exclusion but acknowledges that the distinction can be unclear and lacks explicit delineation in Alabama authority. The practical implications concern policy scope and accurate disclosure of operations: the court reasons that disclosure of recreational-equipment work could have allowed the insurer to add coverage and adjust the premium.

qs.q: The policy states simply that “[the] Insured performs         landscaping.” In short, the Specified Operations provision (fitting         into the gap left by the general coverage provision) describes the         contours or boundaries of coverage—it does not purport to take         away coverage already granted.
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: Thus, the Specified Operations provision is a limitation of         coverage—not an exclusion—and Snell, “as the party seeking         coverage under the Policy, bears the burden [under Alabama law]
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

kps.k: The indemnity and bad-faith holdings reinforce the application-based result without supplying evidence about AI.
kps.d: The court rejects a categorical bar on deciding indemnity before judgment in the underlying action, while acknowledging contrary language in earlier federal decisions and the possibility that later developments can change complaint-dependent coverage determinations. Here, the application independently forecloses coverage, and no material factual dispute requires delay. The bad-faith claim also fails because United lawfully denied coverage and Snell did not establish the requisite investigative misconduct. These are qualified insurance-law holdings, not findings about automated interpretation or verification.

qs.q: In sum, we hold that the duty to indemnify under Alabama         insurance law can, at least under some circumstances, be decided         before the underlying action reaches judgment.
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

qs.q: We also appear to have taken for granted (this time in a published case) that         “the duty to indemnify cannot be determined” under Alabama law “at a         preliminary stage in the proceedings,” (i.e., before judgment) noting that         “district courts in our circuit have declined to address the duty to indemnify         when determining whether there is a duty to defend.” James River Ins.
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

vlens.an: The supplied judicial source supports the cluster’s principal proposition. The court’s coverage decision rests on Snell’s insurance application and controlling Alabama law, so it does not require resolution of the ordinary meaning of “landscaping” or reliance on an LLM. The source also preserves the distinction between the binding grounds of decision and Judge Newsom’s separate interpretive reflections: he joins the court’s opinion in full, while the supplied excerpt only introduces—without substantively presenting—his proposal concerning legal interpretation. The material therefore cannot support broader claims about recommended judicial uses or capabilities of LLMs. The principal internal variation is limited but material: Newsom personally doubts the governing interpretation of the Alabama statute, yet accepts that the court is bound by the state supreme court’s construction. This assessment concerns this curated source alone and should not be generalized to regulators, courts, or professional bodies as a whole.

qs.q: Even taking the term “landscaping” as ambiguous,         construing it in Snell’s favor, and applying Alabama law’s broad         understanding of the causal term “arises out of,” Snell’s claim still         fails.
qs.a: Snell v. United Specialty Insurance Co., 102 F.4th 1208 (11th Cir. 2024) — Judge Newsom's concurrence on LLMs and ordinary meaning · Regulators & courts · 2024

elens.an: The source supports the proposition that the case was resolved through case-specific insurance documents and binding Alabama law, not through LLM use or a definitive ruling on the ordinary meaning of “landscaping.” The central reason is that Snell’s application denied recreational-equipment work, so the claim failed even if “landscaping” were construed favorably to him. The source also supports the synthesis’s evidentiary caution: Newsom’s interpretive reflections appeared in a separate concurrence, while the supplied excerpt ends before any substantive LLM proposal is developed. Material internal variation is limited to Newsom’s personal doubt about the governing statute’s interpretation; he nonetheless joined the opinion in full and accepted controlling state law. The associated indemnity and bad-faith rulings further apply insurance law without adding evidence about AI. Because this facet contains a single curated judicial source, the assessment concerns that source alone and does not imply a broader judicial consensus.

qs.q: Even taking the term “landscaping” as ambiguous,         construing it in Snell’s favor, and applying Alabama law’s broad         understanding of the causal term “arises out of,” Snell’s claim still         fails.
